``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import os
import re
import tempfile
import textwrap
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, Circle, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, offense, defense, routes as r, style, draw_marker, show_animation

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
FIELD_W = 160 / 3
LOOK = "#0f7a55"           # "look here" badges (a darker step of the aqua highlight)
NEW_TINT = "#dcefe6"       # rows that are new in this chapter on the card


def pct(x, nd=0):
    """0.613 -> '61%'."""
    return f"{100 * x:.{nd}f}%"


def blank(ax):
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.grid(False)


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where wide receivers and corners stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def badge(ax, x, y, n, color=LOOK, r=1.15, fs=7.5, z=15):
    """A numbered circle in plot coordinates (equal-aspect axes only)."""
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r, fc=color, ec="white", lw=0.8, zorder=z))
    ax.text(x, y, str(n), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=z + 1)


def fbadge(fld, play, n, at, **kw):
    """A numbered badge at alignment coordinates (d, w)."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    badge(fld.ax, float(x), float(y), n, **kw)


def tag(fld, play, text, at, fs=7.0, ha="center", color=style.INK, bold=False, ec=style.BASELINE):
    """A boxed label at alignment coordinates (d, w), drawn above the players."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color, zorder=14, linespacing=1.12,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=0.6))


def scorebug(fld, play, lines, at, fs=6.6, ha="left"):
    """A small dark scorebug box at (d, w)."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, "\n".join(lines), ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color="white", zorder=16,
                linespacing=1.25, fontweight="bold",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc="#2b2b2b", ec="none"))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ print stand-ins for animations
def snapshot(play, t, ax, lateral, window, notes=(), trails=True):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, with faint trails of where he has been and the ball in flight."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for n in notes:
        q.note(*n)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    no_numbers(fld.ax)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    t0 = play._compile()[1]
    if trails:
        for k, pl in play.players.items():
            if pl.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
                continue
            pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t, 40)])
            if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.4:
                continue
            xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
            col = style.OFFENSE if pl.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
            ls = "-" if pl.side == "off" else (0, (3, 2))
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=1.0, alpha=0.5, ls=ls, zorder=3)
    bx, by = P(*play.ball_position(t))
    thrown = False
    for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:
            thrown = True
            sx, sy = P(*play.ball_position(t_rel))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    if thrown:
        draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)   # before the throw the QB has it: no icon on him
    elif t > 0:
        for who, tgt in play.reads:                               # the quarterback's eyes, until he throws
            (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(*play.position(who, t)), P(*play.position(tgt, t))
            ax.plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
                    zorder=4)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window, notes_at=None, ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    """The print version of an animation: one panel per moment, each titled with what to see."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.36)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        snapshot(play, t, ax, lateral, window, notes=(notes_at or {}).get(i, ()))
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.4)
    return fig


def animate_or_strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window, notes_at=None):
    """Video on the web, a titled frame strip in print."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window, notes_at=notes_at)
        plt.show()
    else:
        show_animation(play, times=times)


def protect(p, linemen=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")):
    """Five linemen set back into pass protection."""
    for k in linemen:
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])


def engage(p, rushers, speed=2.0):
    """Rushers who run into the protection (enough to show a pass rush, no more)."""
    for k in rushers:
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=speed)
```

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting, 2024–2025)"}
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

PCOLS = ["season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "defteam", "play_type", "down", "ydstogo",
         "yardline_100", "pass", "half_seconds_remaining", "score_differential", "qtr", "fixed_drive", "time",
         "yrdln", "desc", "yards_gained", "posteam_score", "defteam_score", "air_yards", "yards_after_catch",
         "qb_dropback", "run_location", "pass_location"]


def load_season(season):
    """Runs and dropbacks with FTN charting (alignment, motion, tempo, rushers) and participation
    (personnel, box count, coverage label) attached."""
    d = pbp([season], columns=PCOLS)
    d = d[d.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & d.down.notna()].copy()
    f = nfl().load_ftn_charting([season]).to_pandas()
    f = f.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
    f["play_id"] = f.play_id.astype(float)
    f = f[["game_id", "play_id", "starting_hash", "qb_location", "n_offense_backfield", "is_motion", "is_no_huddle",
           "is_play_action", "is_screen_pass", "n_pass_rushers", "n_blitzers", "read_thrown",
           "is_qb_out_of_pocket"]]
    p = nfl().load_participation([season]).to_pandas()
    p = p.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
    p["play_id"] = p.play_id.astype(float)
    p = p[["game_id", "play_id", "offense_personnel", "defense_personnel", "defenders_in_box",
           "defense_coverage_type", "defense_man_zone_type", "time_to_throw", "was_pressure", "route"]]
    d["play_id"] = d.play_id.astype(float)
    return d.merge(f, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left").merge(p, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")


def count_pos(s, keys):
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    c = {k: int(v) for v, k in re.findall(r"(\d+) ([A-Z]+)", s)}
    return sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in keys)


def pers_code(s):
    """FTN-era personnel string ('1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 1 TE, 3 WR') -> '11'."""
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return "na"
    c = {k: int(v) for v, k in re.findall(r"(\d+) ([A-Z]+)", s)}
    code = f"{c.get('RB', 0) + c.get('FB', 0)}{c.get('TE', 0)}"
    return code if code in ("10", "11", "12", "13", "21", "22", "01", "02") else "other"


def features(d):
    d = d.copy()
    dist = pd.cut(d.ydstogo, [0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 10, 99], labels=["1", "2", "3", "4-6", "7-10", "11+"]).astype(str)
    d["dd"] = d.down.astype(int).astype(str) + "_" + dist
    d["zone"] = pd.cut(d.yardline_100, [0, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100],
                       labels=["g5", "g10", "rz", "o40", "mid", "own40", "own20"]).astype(str)
    d["score"] = pd.cut(d.score_differential, [-99, -9, -1, 0, 8, 99],
                        labels=["d9+", "d1-8", "tie", "u1-8", "u9+"]).astype(str)
    d["late"] = np.where(d.half_seconds_remaining <= 120, "late", "no")
    d["q4score"] = np.where(d.qtr >= 4, "q4", "no") + d["score"]
    d["pers"] = d.offense_personnel.map(pers_code)
    backs = d.n_offense_backfield.fillna(-1).clip(upper=2).astype(int).astype(str)
    d["formation"] = d.qb_location.fillna("na").astype(str) + backs
    d["motion"] = d.is_motion.fillna(False).astype(bool).astype(str)
    d["tempo"] = d.is_no_huddle.fillna(False).astype(bool).astype(str)
    d["box"] = pd.cut(d.defenders_in_box.fillna(-1), [-2, 0, 5, 6, 7, 99],
                      labels=["na", "5-", "6", "7", "8+"]).astype(str)
    d["dbs"] = d.defense_personnel.map(lambda s: count_pos(s, ("CB", "FS", "SS", "S", "DB")))
    return d


# The checklist steps that can be measured in public data, in checklist order
STEPS = [("Situation", ["dd", "zone", "score", "late", "q4score"]),
         ("+ Personnel", ["pers"]),
         ("+ Formation", ["formation"]),
         ("+ Motion and tempo", ["motion", "tempo"]),
         ("+ Box count", ["box"])]


def design(d, cats, levels=None):
    if levels is None:
        levels = {c: sorted(d[c].unique()) for c in cats}
    cols = [np.ones(len(d))]
    for c in cats:
        for lv in levels[c][1:]:
            cols.append((d[c].values == lv).astype(float))
    return np.column_stack(cols), levels


def fit(X, y, lam=1.0, iters=30):
    """Ridge-penalised logistic regression by Newton's method (numpy only)."""
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w))
        H = X.T @ (X * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]) + lam * np.eye(X.shape[1])
        w -= np.linalg.solve(H, X.T @ (p - y) + lam * w)
    return w


def nested(train):
    models, cats = [], []
    for name, cs in STEPS:
        cats = cats + cs
        X, lv = design(train, cats)
        models.append((name, list(cats), lv, fit(X, train["pass"].values.astype(float))))
    return models


def predict(model, d):
    _, cats, lv, w = model
    X, _ = design(d, cats, lv)
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w))


S24 = features(load_season(2024))
S25 = features(load_season(2025))
TR = S24[S24.season_type == "REG"]
TE = S25[S25.season_type == "REG"]

# What each step is worth: learn on 2024, score on 2025
MODELS = nested(TR)
WORTH = [dict(step="Always guess pass", acc=float(TE["pass"].mean()), hi=np.nan, hi_acc=np.nan)]
for m in MODELS:
    p_ = predict(m, TE)
    y_ = TE["pass"].values
    right = (p_ >= 0.5) == y_
    hi = np.maximum(p_, 1 - p_) >= 0.8
    WORTH.append(dict(step=m[0], acc=float(right.mean()), hi=float(hi.mean()), hi_acc=float(right[hi].mean())))
W = {w_["step"]: w_ for w_ in WORTH}

# Confidence bands after the first three steps (situation, personnel, formation)
pF = predict(MODELS[2], TE)
cF = np.maximum(pF, 1 - pF)
rF = (pF >= 0.5) == TE["pass"].values
BANDS = []
for lo, hi_ in [(0.5, 0.6), (0.6, 0.7), (0.7, 0.8), (0.8, 0.9), (0.9, 1.01)]:
    m_ = (cF >= lo) & (cF < hi_)
    BANDS.append(dict(lo=lo, hi=min(hi_, 1.0), share=float(m_.mean()), acc=float(rF[m_].mean()),
                      conf=float(cF[m_].mean())))


def prate(mask):
    return float(TE.loc[mask, "pass"].mean())


RATE = dict(
    all=prate(TE.down > 0),
    first10=prate((TE.down == 1) & (TE.ydstogo == 10)),
    third7=prate((TE.down == 3) & TE.ydstogo.between(7, 10)),
    third46gun11=prate((TE.down == 3) & TE.ydstogo.between(4, 6) & (TE.pers == "11") & (TE.qb_location == "S")),
    third3gun=prate((TE.down == 3) & (TE.ydstogo == 3) & (TE.qb_location == "S")),
    third12uc=prate((TE.down == 3) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2) & (TE.qb_location == "U")),
    third12gun=prate((TE.down == 3) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2) & (TE.qb_location == "S")),
    second12=prate((TE.down == 2) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2)),
    second12gun11=prate((TE.down == 2) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2) & (TE.pers == "11") & (TE.qb_location == "S")),
    second12gun11nh=prate((TE.down == 2) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2) & (TE.pers == "11")
                          & (TE.qb_location == "S") & (TE.tempo == "True")),
    first21uc=prate((TE.down == 1) & (TE.ydstogo == 10) & (TE.pers == "21") & (TE.qb_location == "U")),
    first21uc8=prate((TE.down == 1) & (TE.ydstogo == 10) & (TE.pers == "21") & (TE.qb_location == "U")
                     & (TE["box"] == "8+")),
    first12uc=prate((TE.down == 1) & (TE.ydstogo == 10) & (TE.pers == "12") & (TE.qb_location == "U")),
    empty=prate(TE["formation"] == "S0"),
    gun=prate(TE.qb_location == "S"), pistol=prate(TE.qb_location == "P"), uc=prate(TE.qb_location == "U"),
    nohuddle=prate(TE.tempo == "True"),
)
LOOK6 = ((TE.down == 2) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2) & (TE.pers == "11") & (TE.qb_location == "S")
         & (TE.n_offense_backfield == 1) & (TE.motion == "True") & (TE["box"] == "6"))
RATE["look6"] = prate(LOOK6)
N_LOOK6 = int(LOOK6.sum())
N_SECOND12NH = int(((TE.down == 2) & TE.ydstogo.between(1, 2) & (TE.pers == "11") & (TE.qb_location == "S")
                    & (TE.tempo == "True")).sum())
N_FIRST21UC8 = int(((TE.down == 1) & (TE.ydstogo == 10) & (TE.pers == "21") & (TE.qb_location == "U")
                    & (TE["box"] == "8+")).sum())

# Rushers and coverage on dropbacks (2025 regular season)
DBK = S25[(S25.season_type == "REG") & (S25.qb_dropback == 1) & (S25.n_pass_rushers > 0)].copy()
DBK["five"] = (DBK.n_pass_rushers >= 5).astype(float)
COV = DBK[DBK.defense_man_zone_type.isin(["MAN_COVERAGE", "ZONE_COVERAGE"])].copy()
COV["man"] = (COV.defense_man_zone_type == "MAN_COVERAGE").astype(float)


def rush5(mask):
    return float(DBK.loc[mask, "five"].mean())


RUSH = dict(all=rush5(DBK.down > 0), third46=rush5((DBK.down == 3) & DBK.ydstogo.between(4, 6)),
            third7=rush5((DBK.down == 3) & DBK.ydstogo.between(7, 10)))
MAN_ALL = float(COV["man"].mean())
MAN_RZ = float(COV.loc[COV.yardline_100 <= 20, "man"].mean())
MAN_OPEN = float(COV.loc[COV.yardline_100 > 20, "man"].mean())


def uc_habits(T):
    """How often a team lines up under center, throws from there, and makes those throws play-action."""
    U = T[T.qb_location == "U"]
    return dict(share=float((T.qb_location == "U").mean()), pass_=float(U["pass"].mean()),
                pa=float(U.loc[U["pass"] == 1, "is_play_action"].mean()))


UC_LG, UC_LA = uc_habits(TE), uc_habits(TE[TE.posteam == "LA"])
M12 = (TE.down == 1) & (TE.pers == "12") & (TE.qb_location == "U")
RATE["first12uc_sea"] = prate(M12 & (TE.posteam == "SEA"))
RATE["first12uc_all"] = prate(M12)
N_12UC_SEA = int((M12 & (TE.posteam == "SEA")).sum())

# Field or boundary? FTN's hash is from the offense's view (screens go to the wide side, away from it)
HSH = TE[TE.starting_hash.isin(["L", "R"])]
TO_FIELD = (((HSH.starting_hash == "L") & (HSH.run_location.eq("right") | HSH.pass_location.eq("right")))
            | ((HSH.starting_hash == "R") & (HSH.run_location.eq("left") | HSH.pass_location.eq("left"))))
WIDE = HSH.run_location.isin(["left", "right"]) | HSH.pass_location.isin(["left", "right"])
SCR = WIDE & (HSH.is_screen_pass == True)  # noqa: E712
RUNW = WIDE & (HSH.play_type == "run")
FIELD = dict(screen=float(TO_FIELD[SCR].mean()), run=float(TO_FIELD[RUNW].mean()))


def brier(c, q):
    """Expected Brier score per call when you say c and the call comes true at rate q."""
    return q * (1 - c) ** 2 + (1 - q) * c ** 2


def buckets(d):
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=d.index)
    dist = pd.cut(d.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 99], labels=["1-3", "4-6", "7+"]).astype(str)
    out["b_dd"] = d.down.astype(int).clip(upper=3).astype(str) + "_" + dist
    out["b_rz"] = np.where(d.yardline_100 <= 20, "rz", "open")
    out["b_db"] = d.dbs.fillna(5).clip(4, 6).astype(int).astype(str)
    return out


for t_ in (DBK, COV):
    t_[["b_dd", "b_rz", "b_db"]] = buckets(t_)


def lookup(table, col, row, nmin=60):
    """Base rate for this down-distance, field zone and number of DBs, backing off to coarser cells."""
    for keys in (("b_dd", "b_rz", "b_db"), ("b_dd", "b_rz"), ("b_dd",)):
        m_ = np.ones(len(table), bool)
        for k in keys:
            m_ &= table[k].values == row[k]
        if m_.sum() >= nmin:
            return float(table.loc[m_, col].mean())
    return float(table[col].mean())


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the film-room drive
DRV = S25[(S25.game_id == "2025_21_LA_SEA") & (S25.posteam == "SEA") & (S25.fixed_drive == 15)]
DRV = DRV.sort_values("play_id").reset_index(drop=True)
TRACE = nested(pd.concat([TR, TE]))           # trained on the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons
for i_, m in enumerate(TRACE):
    DRV[f"p{i_}"] = predict(m, DRV)
DRV["p"] = DRV[f"p{len(TRACE) - 1}"]


def conf_of(p):
    return int(np.clip(5 * round(100 * max(p, 1 - p) / 5), 50, 90))


DRV["call"] = np.where(DRV.p >= 0.5, "Pass", "Run")
DRV["conf"] = DRV.p.map(conf_of)
bk = buckets(DRV)
DRV["p_man"] = [lookup(COV, "man", bk.loc[i_]) for i_ in DRV.index]
DRV["p_five"] = [lookup(DBK, "five", bk.loc[i_]) for i_ in DRV.index]
DRV["cov_call"] = np.where(DRV.p_man >= 0.5, "man", "zone")
DRV["cov_conf"] = DRV.p_man.map(conf_of)
DRV["rush_call"] = np.where(DRV.p_five >= 0.5, "5+", "4")
DRV["rush_conf"] = DRV.p_five.map(conf_of)
DRV["is_pass"] = DRV["pass"] == 1
DRV["hit"] = (DRV.call == "Pass") == DRV.is_pass
DRV["cov_hit"] = np.where(DRV.is_pass, (DRV.cov_call == "man") == (DRV.defense_man_zone_type == "MAN_COVERAGE"), np.nan)
DRV["rush_hit"] = np.where(DRV.is_pass, (DRV.rush_call == "5+") == (DRV.n_pass_rushers >= 5), np.nan)
RESULT = {2550: "Holani run, +3", 2572: "Walker run, −2", 2594: "Kupp catch, +12 (1st)",
          2619: "Walker run, +11 (1st)", 2641: "Holani catch, +9", 2666: "Smith-Njigba screen, +12 (1st)",
          2691: "Play-action, Barner +7", 2716: "Incomplete to Bobo", 2739: "Kupp, 13-yard TD"}
DRV["result"] = DRV.play_id.map(lambda x: RESULT[int(x)])
D = DRV.set_index(DRV.index + 1)           # D.loc[3] is the third snap of the drive
N_HIT = int(DRV.hit.sum())
N_L2 = int(np.nansum(DRV.cov_hit) + np.nansum(DRV.rush_hit))
N_L2_ALL = int(2 * DRV.is_pass.sum())
N_COV = int(np.nansum(DRV.cov_hit))
N_RUSH = int(np.nansum(DRV.rush_hit))
N_PASS = int(DRV.is_pass.sum())


_a8 = int(D.loc[8, "air_yards"])
AIR8 = f"{abs(_a8)} yard{'s' if abs(_a8) != 1 else ''} {'behind' if _a8 < 0 else 'past'} the line"
Q90 = BANDS[4]["acc"]
BRIER = dict(c90=brier(0.90, Q90), honest=brier(Q90, Q90), c99=brier(0.99, Q90))


def snap_conf(i):
    return f"{D.loc[i, 'call'].lower()}, {D.loc[i, 'conf']}%"
```

**The NFC Championship Game, January 25, 2026.** Third quarter, 8:23 to play, and the Rams have just
pulled within four points. Seattle faces third-and-9 at its own 36, and on a typical broadcast the replay of the run that just
lost two yards would still be rolling as the Seahawks come back to the line: one running back, one
tight end, three receivers, quarterback in the shotgun. The Rams answer with six defensive backs
and only five men near the ball. You have about twenty seconds. Most viewers spend them waiting for
the snap. A coach in the booth spends them asking a set of questions in the same order he asks them
before every snap: *What does the situation demand? Who's on the field? How are they lined up? What
does the defense do when someone moves? How many are in the box? How many are deep? Where is the help?
Is anyone coming?* And then he says out loud what he thinks will happen, and how sure he is. This
chapter puts the whole course into that routine. By the end of it you'll run the same questions in
the same order, and you'll keep score.

**You'll be able to…**

- Run the master pre-snap checklist in about twenty seconds, in order: situation → personnel →
  formation and strength → motion response → box → shell → leverage → pressure tells → prediction,
  and know which steps to keep when the offense goes fast.
- Use the full tells catalogue (linemen's stance and weight, the back's depth and offset, pistol
  against shotgun, receiver splits, the tight end's stance, linebacker depth, defensive back depth
  and leverage, safety width), saying for each what it usually means and why it leaks, and, where public
  data can measure it, how often it lies.
- Say what each step of the checklist is worth, from 2024–2025 data, and why the later steps answer
  different questions from run or pass.
- Make layered predictions (run or pass first, then the coverage family, the rush, where the ball
  goes or which way the run hits), each with a stated confidence between 50% and 90%.
- Follow a complete playoff drive snap by snap the way a coach in the booth does, and keep the log
  that [Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) will score.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This is a Level 5 chapter: it assembles the course rather than adding new schemes. One line on each
piece it leans on hardest:

- **In-game adjustments and tempo** ([In-Game Adjustments, Tempo, and the Sideline Battle](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)):
  [tempo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tempo) is how fast the offense gets to the line and snaps; a
  [hurry-up offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hurry-up-offense) snaps as fast as it can, and the
  [substitution freeze](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-freeze) means a defense that
  can't match a substitution has to play with the eleven it has.
- **The clock and fourth down** ([The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)):
  in the [two-minute drill](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-minute-drill) and the
  [four-minute offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-minute-offense) the clock decides much of
  the play call, and fourth down is a decision of its own.
- **Tendencies from data** ([Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage from Charting Data](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)):
  [xpass](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-xpass) (expected pass rate) is the chance of a pass given the
  situation alone, and [PROE](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-proe) (pass rate over expected) is how
  much a team throws beyond it; a [tendency](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency) is a pattern in
  what it calls from a given look.
- **The habit** ([How to Watch a Broadcast Like You Mean It](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
  a [tell](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tell) is a pre-snap clue that shifts the odds, never a
  guarantee; the [prediction log](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-prediction-log) is your record of
  calls, with a confidence column. The "checklist so far" cards in Parts 2, 4, 6 and 7 are the drafts of
  the card this chapter finishes.

## Twenty seconds, a hundred clues

Start with the problem the checklist solves: there's far more to see before a snap than anyone can
see, and very little time. The play clock is 40 seconds, starting the moment the previous play is
whistled dead (25 seconds after some stoppages, such as a timeout or a change of possession).[^clock]
On a broadcast the first part of that is usually spent on replays of the play that just ended. The
offense huddles while its play-caller talks to the quarterback through the helmet radio, which goes
silent with 15 seconds left on the play clock.[^radio] Then the players walk to the line, set, maybe
move someone in motion, and the ball is snapped. A team that huddles spends most of what is left of the
play clock at the line; a team in tempo can snap within a few seconds of setting.

So your budget is roughly twenty seconds, from the moment the scorebug updates to the snap, and the
camera won't show you all of it. Within those twenty seconds, information doesn't arrive all at once.
It arrives in a fixed order, because the game produces it in a fixed order:

That ordering is the first reason the checklist has the shape it has: **each step is asked when its
answer is visible.** There is no point hunting for the safeties while the offense is still in the
huddle; they haven't settled. There is every point in reading the scorebug during the replay, because
the situation is already fixed and nothing else is.

The second reason is less obvious and more important: **each answer changes what the next clue
means.** A safety walking down to eight yards on third-and-9 is a defense guarding the sticks; the same
move on first-and-10 against two tight ends is an eighth man for the run. A receiver tightening his split
means one thing from a team that runs on 70% of its snaps in that look and another from a team that
throws on 70%. Clues aren't independent bits of evidence to be added up. They are answers to questions,
and the questions come in an order. Read the box before you know the personnel, and you'll miscount it.
Read the shell before you know the down, and you won't know what you're looking at.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: a checklist, of all things"}
A checklist sounds like the opposite of expertise. Surely the expert just *sees* it? But the
professions that have to perform under time pressure without missing anything (pilots running a
pre-flight check, surgical teams before an incision) settled long ago on short, ordered checklists, and
not because their people were beginners. A checklist offloads the *remembering* so that attention is
free for the *judging*.[^gawande] Yours is the kind Gawande calls *do-confirm*: you run it from memory,
then glance at the card to make sure you skipped nothing. A quarterback's pre-snap routine (count the
safeties, find the Mike, know where the hot throw goes) is a checklist too. Yours fights the same enemy: the
eye goes to the most interesting thing on the screen (usually the quarterback) and stays there, while the
clue that decided the play happens forty yards away.

What it gives up: a fixed routine is slower than a glance, and on the snaps where the offense hurries
you'll have to cut it short. That's why the card has a short version.
:::

Against the last draft, at the end of
[Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd), three
things changed. The protection question has been folded into the pressure step, so there are nine pre-snap
steps, not ten. Each tell sits in the step where you'd see it (alignment tells in step 3, depth and leverage
in step 7, pressure in step 8). And the prediction is a step of its own, with a number: "pass, 80%" before
the snap, not "I had a feeling" after it. The rest of this section walks the nine steps in order: what you're
looking at, what it tells you, and why it sits where it does.

### Step 1: situation, the base rate

Down, distance, field zone, clock, score, timeouts. You learned to read the scorebug in five seconds in
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), and the situational
chapters (Part 10, from [Third Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd) to
[The Clock](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)) taught you what each situation
does to the play-caller. The output of step 1 is a number: the **base rate**, how often offenses throw in
this situation before anyone has lined up. That is what [xpass](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-xpass)
measures, and it's the anchor every later step moves.

Add one more thing a coach reads first: **where the ball is spotted.** On a
[hash](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hash-marks), one side of the formation has far more room (the
[field side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-side)) than the other (the
[boundary side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-boundary-side)). Defenses set their strength, rotations and
blitzes by it, and offenses put their formations and perimeter plays into the room: in 2025, screens thrown
from a hash went to the wide side 63% of the time.[^hash]

You don't need a model in your head, just a few landmarks from the 2025 regular season:[^rates]

| Situation | Pass rate, 2025 | What it means for your call |
|:--------------|:-------:|:----------------------|
| All snaps | 60% | "Always pass" is the floor any reader has to beat |
| 1st-and-10 | 50% | A coin flip until the formation speaks |
| 2nd-and-1 or 2 | 31% | Mostly runs, but this is where shots happen |
| 3rd-and-1 or 2, under center | 19% | Run, and the formation says so |
| 3rd-and-1 or 2, shotgun | 52% | A genuine coin flip |
| 3rd-and-7 to 10 | 94% | Pass; spend your seconds on the second layer |
| No-huddle, any down | 70% | Mostly offenses that are behind; under one in five comes in a two-minute drill |

Two things to say alongside the number. First, **is this a clock situation?** In the
[two-minute drill](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-minute-drill) and the
[four-minute offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-minute-offense) the clock calls half the plays,
and [The Clock](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) gave you a separate set of
questions for them (in bounds or out, timeout or spike, kneel or not). Second, **does this team break the base
rate?** That is [PROE](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-proe). Before kickoff, copy three numbers per team
from the one-page scouting report in
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) onto your sheet: its PROE, its
pass rate from under center, and its play-action rate. A team with a high PROE moves your 50% first down
toward 55 or 60 before you've seen a thing.

Why first: it's the only clue complete during the replay, and the biggest single clue there is.

### Step 2: personnel, and the match

Count the backs and tight ends as the offense runs on, and watch who runs *off*. The two digits
(11, 12, 21, 13) were the first thing [Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
taught, because personnel is chosen before the formation: the play-caller sends in a group, and the group
limits what the formation can be. Then notice *which* players came on, not only how many. Defenses substitute
for players as well as for numbers: a star receiver on the field can draw a nickel even when the digits say
two tight ends (you'll see exactly that on the drive below). A defense in nickel against 12 personnel has a
defensive back where a linebacker usually stands, and the offense will often run at him; a defense in base
against 11 personnel has a linebacker who may have to cover a slot receiver, and the offense will often throw
at him. This is also where you notice **tempo**: an offense that hurries to the line without substituting
after a big gain, or right after the defense subbed into a run-stopping group, is usually hunting a mismatch
the [substitution freeze](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-freeze) has locked in.

Why second: personnel is visible before the formation is, and it's the context for what the formation shows.
On its own it adds surprisingly little to a run-or-pass call; its value is in what it sets up.

### Step 3: formation, strength and the offensive tells

This is the richest step. Where is the quarterback: under center, in the shotgun, in the pistol? Where is
the back, how deep, offset to which side? Where is the tight end, on the line or off it, in a three-point
stance or standing up? How wide are the receivers? Which side is the
[formation strength](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-formation-strength)?

Strength matters because both sides organise around it. The defense sets its front and usually its safety
rotation to the strong side, and the offense's runs and its best route combinations usually go there too.
But "strong" is a dialect, not a fact: a defense may declare it to the tight end, to the side with more
receivers, or to the field, and its choice decides which way the front and the rotation set
([Formation Rules and Vocabulary](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)
showed all three). When the tight end is on one side and three receivers are on the other, watch which way the
linebackers shift; that tells you which dialect this defense speaks.

The vocabulary came from [Formation Rules and Vocabulary](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd),
the families of plays each look goes with from the run-game and passing-game parts, and
[the tells catalogue](#the-tells-catalogue) below collects every alignment clue in one place.

Why third: the offense has to show its formation before the defense commits to its final picture, and the
defense's last-second picture is a *response* to it. Read the formation first and you'll understand what
the defense does next.

### Step 4: motion response

When a player moves before the snap, watch the defense, not the man in motion. A defender who
[travels](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-travel-man-defender-follows-motion) across the formation with him
suggests man coverage; defenders who [bump](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bump-defensive-adjustment) a
spot over suggest zone; a safety who [spins](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-safety-rotation-on-motion)
down turns two-high into one-high. That's the
[man/zone indicator](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-zone-indicator) from
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd). Then ask the
offensive question: is he still moving when the ball is snapped
([motion at the snap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion-at-the-snap))? A jet motion at full speed is a
run threat, or a decoy for one, to that side.

You will get to use this step on most snaps. PFF's charting had a shift or motion on 63.9% of 2025 snaps,
the highest in its series, and every team but the Giants used one on at least half its plays.[^motion]

Treat the answer as a lean, not a read. Defenses know this indicator as well as you do: a man defense can
bump over and swap assignments (an exchange), and a pattern-matching zone can send a defender across with the
motion, which is how [Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) showed the
indicator lying. File the motion response next to leverage and the shell; when all three agree, believe it.

Why fourth: motion only happens after the offense sets, and its whole point is to make the defense answer
a question before the snap. The answer is a clue for steps 5 to 7.

### Step 5: the box

Count the defenders in the [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box) and compare them with the blockers
([box count](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box-count)). Six blockers against six defenders is a fair fight
for a run; six against eight means two defenders will be unblocked, which is why an offense that sees eight
usually throws or checks to a run away from the extra man
([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)). A light
box (six or fewer) against a shotgun offense is the classic invitation for a run or an
[RPO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rpo).

Why fifth: the box isn't final until motion has settled it. Count too early and you'll count a safety who
is about to leave, or miss one who is about to arrive.

### Step 6: the shell

One-high or two-high? Then the details: each safety's depth (13 yards is deep, 8 is down), his width (on the
hash or inside it, or out wide), and any creep in the last seconds of the play clock. This was the spine of
the coverage chapters, and [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
was about why the shell you see is often not the coverage you get. The numbers show the gap. After the snap,
NFL Next Gen Stats measured two-high coverage on 42.0% of dropbacks in 2025, the highest since it began
tracking in 2018.[^twohigh] Before the snap, defenses show two-high far more often than that: preparing for
Seattle's defense before Super Bowl LX, the Patriots' offensive coordinator, Josh McDaniels, said 65 of 70
snaps would "look the same before the ball's snapped"[^mcdaniels]
([Fangio's Two-High Revolution](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)). The distance between
the shell shown and the coverage played is the disguise. So two-high before the snap is not a tell by itself;
the tell is which of the two safeties is shallower, narrower or moving.

Why sixth: safeties are the last defenders to settle and the most likely to be lying, so you read them as
late as you can.

### Step 7: leverage and depth

Look at the corners: pressed at the line or off at seven yards; on the receiver's inside shoulder or his
outside. [Leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside) tells you what the defender is
protecting and so where his help is: a corner playing outside leverage is giving up the inside because
someone (a safety in the middle, a linebacker underneath) is there to take it. Then the linebackers' depth:
at four and a half to five and a half yards they are playing the run and the short middle; creeping to three,
they may be coming; backing out to eight before the snap on a passing down, they are getting a head start into
zone drops.

Why seventh: leverage is the last thing a defense adjusts, and it only makes sense after you know the shell.
An inside-leverage corner with two deep safeties means something different from the same corner with one.

### Step 8: pressure tells

How many defenders are at or near the line, and could any of them drop? Linebackers mugging the A gaps,
a safety or nickel back walked up beside the end, a defensive lineman sitting back on his heels: these are
the [pressure look](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure-look) tells from the pressure chapters. Then
the count that caps everything: **how many players are deep?** Two deep safeties and two off corners leave seven
to rush and cover underneath, and a defense almost never rushes six with only one underneath. Six-man pressure
is real, but it comes as [Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0), man-to-man with nobody deep,
and that needs the safeties to walk down first; if they're still at 12 yards at the snap, six isn't coming.

Finish with the offense's side, which is the easiest pressure tell to see on a broadcast: **the offense
reacting.** The center pointing and calling out the middle linebacker, the quarterback stepping up to reset
the protection or turning to the sideline, a back sliding across to the other side of the quarterback: each
says the offense sees a pressure and has changed who blocks whom. Then ask which way the line will
[slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection) and where the
[hot route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) goes.

Why eighth: pressure looks are deliberately last-second. Defenses walk up late so the offense has as
little time as possible to change its protection, and you get the same late look the quarterback does.

### Step 9: call it, with a number

Say it out loud before the snap: run or pass, and how sure you are. Then, if you have a second left, one
more layer: the coverage family, how many will rush, or where the ball should go. This is the step this
chapter adds, and it gets [its own section](#stated-confidence-putting-a-number-on-it) below. The rule is
simple: the call is made *before* the snap, or it doesn't count.

## What each step is worth

How much does each step actually help? For the run-or-pass call, we can measure it. Charting services
record, for every NFL snap, much of what steps 1 to 5 ask about: the situation, the personnel, the
quarterback's alignment and the number of backs, whether there was motion, whether the offense huddled,
and how many defenders were in the box. (Steps 6 to 8 aren't in public data: nobody charts pre-snap safety
depth or corner leverage for every snap.) So we can do what a reader would do: learn from one season what
each combination of clues usually meant, then call every snap of the next season, adding one step at a time.

::: {#cell-fig-checklist-worth .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.75), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.15, 1]))
names = [w_["step"] for w_ in WORTH]
ys = np.arange(len(names))[::-1]
cols = [style.MUTED] + [style.OFFENSE] * (len(names) - 1)
cols[3] = style.THIRD                          # the formation step: the big jump
accs = [w_["acc"] for w_ in WORTH]
a1.barh(ys, accs, color=cols, height=0.6, zorder=2)
for y_, v in zip(ys, accs):
    a1.text(v + 0.004, y_, pct(v, 1), va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK)
a1.set_xlim(0.55, 0.81)
a1.set_yticks(ys, names, fontsize=7.6)
a1.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
a1.set_xlabel("run/pass calls right, 2025", fontsize=7.6)
a1.set_title("Accuracy", fontsize=8.6)
a1.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
his = [0 if np.isnan(w_["hi"]) else w_["hi"] for w_ in WORTH]
a2.barh(ys, his, color=cols, height=0.6, zorder=2)
for y_, w_ in zip(ys, WORTH):
    if np.isnan(w_["hi"]):
        a2.text(0.01, y_, "never sure", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
    else:
        a2.text(w_["hi"] + 0.008, y_, f"{pct(w_['hi'])}  ({pct(w_['hi_acc'])} right)", va="center", ha="left",
                fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK)
a2.set_xlim(0, 0.72)
a2.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
a2.set_xlabel("share of snaps called at 80%+", fontsize=7.6)
a2.set_title("Confident calls", fontsize=8.6)
a2.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

Three lessons hide in that chart.[^worth]

**The situation is most of the call.** Down, distance, field zone, score and clock take you from
60% ("always pass") to 69%.
That is the step a casual fan skips because it feels too obvious to count.

**The formation is the one big jump after it.** Adding the quarterback's alignment and the number of backs
lifts the model to 75%, and, as important, raises the share of snaps it
can call at 80% confidence or better from 28% to
44%. Personnel alone added little on top of the situation (about
0\.5 points), because most of what the personnel
tells you, the formation tells you again, more precisely.

**Motion, tempo and the box add almost nothing to run or pass.** Together they move the needle by
0\.3 points. Not because they're useless: they answer *other questions*. Motion identifies the coverage; the box says
whether a run, if it comes, has a chance (and partly repeats the formation, since the defense set it in reply).
The same is likely true of the steps nobody charts: safety depth and corner leverage say little about
*whether* the offense will throw, and a great deal about *where* and *against what*.

That changes how you should spend your twenty seconds. **By the end of step 3 your run-or-pass call is
essentially made. Steps 4 to 8 are for the second layer**: the coverage, the pressure, where the ball should
go, which way the run will hit. A reader who spends all twenty seconds agonising over run or pass is using
the expensive steps on the cheap question.

Here is the whole catalogue as a reference table: what each tell usually means, *why* it leaks (a tell
that has no physical or tactical reason behind it won't survive a self-scout), how much to trust it, and
whether you'll see it live or only on the replay.

| # | Tell | Usually means | Why it leaks | How far to trust it; where you'll see it |
|:-|:--------|:------------------|:--------------|:-------------|
| 1 | Linemen's stance and weight | Heavy hand, weight forward: run. Light hand, hips back, a tackle's outside foot staggered or a two-point stance, the line set a little off the ball: pass. A guard with less weight on his hand, cheated back a few inches or with his heel turned: a pull, so a gap run | A 320-pound man can't explode forward from his heels or kick back from his fingertips, and a puller needs a head start sideways | Medium on early downs; quiet on short yardage, when everyone is heavy. *Replay (end zone); live only on close-ups.* |
| 2 | Back's depth and offset | Shotgun runs usually cross the quarterback's face, away from the back's side; a deeper back wants time to read | The handoff path points one way; reading blocks needs a running start | Medium for direction; weak for run or pass. *Live, every snap.* |
| 3 | Shotgun, pistol or under center | Shotgun mostly pass (79% in 2025); pistol and under center mostly run | Each alignment is built for a family of plays | Strong for run/pass, but under-center passes are mostly play-action, built to exploit this tell. *Live, every snap.* |
| 4 | Receiver split | Reduced: a crack block, a short crosser, or room to break outside. Wide: an isolated route, deep or breaking inside | Receivers set their split to make their job easier | Weak: tells you *where* to look more than *what*. *Live on the wide shot; replay otherwise.* |
| 5 | Tight end's stance | Hand down on the line: block likely. Standing, flexed: route likely | Blocking starts low; releasing starts tall | Weak; many teams stand the tight end up on every snap. *Live.* |
| 6 | Defensive lineman's width and stance | Wide-aligned edge: pass rush. A lineman sitting back: stunt or drop | A wide rusher has a straight path to the quarterback; the looper on a stunt (the lineman who swings around his teammate) needs his weight back to go sideways | Medium on obvious passing downs. *Replay; live from the end-zone shot.* |
| 7 | Linebacker depth | Creeping to 3 yards late: blitz or a downhill run fit. Backing out early: zone drop | A blitzer needs a head start; a dropper needs depth | Medium; walking up is also a bluff. *Live, on the wide shot.* |
| 8 | Nickel's spot | Apexed: run support or zone. Tight on the slot: man, or a nickel blitz | Man coverage needs proximity; an apex keeps both jobs in reach | Medium. *Live.* |
| 9 | Corner depth and leverage | Press: man or a hard corner. Off with outside leverage: help inside (a deep middle safety). Inside leverage: usually man, with no help inside (the sideline is his help) or a safety over the top | A defender takes away the side where he has no help | Medium; leverage also follows the play-call's coverage of the week. *Replay (skycam); live on the wide shot.* |
| 10 | Safety depth and width | Deep and at normal width, 8 to 10 yards from the middle: a deep half or quarter. The shallower one, the one pinched to the hash, or the one moving: the rotation | A safety can't cover more than about eight to ten yards of ground between the snap and the throw | Strong *when it moves late*; disguise is the norm. *Top edge of the TV picture; skycam replay.* |

A few of these deserve a sentence more than the table can give them.

**The back's offset is a direction tell, not a run-or-pass tell.** Shotgun runs most often send the back
across the quarterback's face, because the mesh (the moment the ball is handed off) happens while the back is
moving across. A back offset to the right usually runs left. But the same offset is where a back sets up
to pass-protect against a rusher from that side, so it tells you *which way* a run goes far more than
*whether* there will be one. (No public charting records the back's offset, so this one you'll have to
calibrate in your own log.)

**The run's scheme has one pre-snap tell, and it's on a guard.** A gap scheme needs a puller, and a guard who
is about to pull sideways often sets up for it: less weight on his hand, a few inches deeper than his
neighbours, his heel turned toward where he's going. Zone has no such tell before the snap; you confirm it *at*
the snap, when the whole line steps the same way together ([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)).

**The split tell is a *where*, not a *what*.** A [reduced split](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reduced-split)
helps three different jobs (a [crack block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block), a shorter crossing
route, room to break outside), so it can't say which is coming. But when a receiver tightens his split on a run
look, watch the defender inside him: that's the man he's coming to block.

**Leverage points at the help.** A defender usually lines up to take away the side where he has no help,
and funnels the receiver toward the side where he has some. So a corner with outside leverage and a single
safety in the middle is telling you the safety is his help. Inside leverage is the man-coverage look, and it
comes in two kinds. With nobody in the middle ([Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0), much
press Cover 1), the corner takes away the quick inside throw himself and uses the sideline as his help. With
two safeties deep, he can sit inside and trail the receiver
([trail technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trail-technique)) because a safety is over the top: that's
[2-Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-man). Read leverage as an arrow pointing at the help, and the
coverage family usually follows.

**Safety width is the most underused tell.** Everyone counts deep safeties; few look at how far apart they
are. NFL hash marks are only about three yards either side of the middle of the field, so use the numbers as
your ruler. A two-high safety at normal width, eight to ten yards from the middle (about halfway between the
hash and the top of the numbers), has a deep half or deep quarter to cover and can't reach the deep middle in
time. A safety pinched to the hash or inside it, within three to five yards of the middle, *can*, and the one
standing shallower than his partner can come down. That asymmetry, not the two-high picture itself, is how you
see a rotation coming.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"NFL players are too good to have tells." Every player has tendencies, because the best way to do a job
quickly is to start in the position the job needs. What separates good teams from bad ones isn't the absence
of tells, it's what they do about them. Every staff [self-scouts](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-self-scout)
its own film looking for the clue an opponent could read, and then decides whether to break it, hide it, or
keep it as bait ([Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)).
The Rams' under-center passing in 2025 is the textbook bait: they lined up under center on
59% of their snaps (the league: 34%), threw on
40% of those (the league: 31%), and made
81% of those throws play-action. The alignment says run, so the linebackers step up,
and the pass goes behind them. A tell that is right 70% of the time is still worth using.
You just shouldn't be 95% sure of it.
:::

## Stated confidence: putting a number on it

Step 9 asks for a number, and this is where the course's most important habit gets its name. A
[**stated confidence**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stated-confidence) is the probability you attach to a
prediction before the snap, said or written as a number rather than a feeling: not "probably a pass" but
"pass, 75%." The prediction log has had a confidence column since Part 1. From here on, it is not optional.

Why a number, rather than just the call?

1. **It separates a read from a guess, over many calls.** A single miss tells you almost nothing: one 90%
   call in ten *should* miss. A pile of them is different. If your 90% calls miss one time in three, you're
   misreading something; if your 55% calls miss half the time, you were honestly unsure, and you said so.
   Without the number, your log can't tell those two patterns apart.
2. **It forces you to use the base rate.** You can't say "80%" for a pass on first-and-10 without asking
   what moved you from 50. If nothing did, the honest number is 50 to 55.
3. **It can be scored.** A forecaster who says "70% chance of rain" isn't wrong when it stays dry; she's
   wrong if, across all her 70% days, it rains on nine in ten, or on three in ten. Your calls work the same
   way: a 70% call should come true about seven times in ten. The next chapter,
   [Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd), scores the season's log that way, with a
   [Brier score](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-brier-score) (the average squared gap between your stated
   confidence and what happened) and a [calibration](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-calibration) plot (do
   your 70% calls come true about 70% of the time?). Researchers who study forecasters have found that
   saying the number, rather than a word like "probably", is itself one of the habits that makes forecasters
   better.[^tetlock]

How do you choose the number? Start from the base rate of step 1, move it with the strong clues (the formation
is the big one), and then respect two limits:

- **Never below 50.** Your call is whichever side you think is more likely, so its confidence is at least
  50%. A 50% call is perfectly honest: it says "I have nothing", and logging it is better than skipping the
  snap.
- **Rarely above 90.** Offenses choose when to break their tendencies, and the snaps that break them are the
  ones built to fool you. Even the most lopsided situations leave room for a surprise: third-and-7 to 10 is a
  pass 94% of the time, not 100%.

What does a well-judged spread of confidences look like? Here is the model from the previous section
(steps 1 to 3 only: situation, personnel and formation) on every 2025 snap, grouped by how sure it was:

That chart is the target for your own log. When the model says 70 to 80%, it's right
71% of the time; when it says 90% or more, it's right 94%
of the time. Nobody expects a person to match a model learned on
33,000 snaps, but the *shape* is the goal: confident where the situation is lopsided, modest everywhere
else, and right about as often as you claimed.[^bands]

But look at the top band: on a fifth of snaps the model was right 94% of the time.
Doesn't a cap at 90 make you *under*confident there? A little, and that's the point: the two mistakes don't
cost the same. On a call that comes true 94% of the time, the
[Brier score](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-brier-score) the next chapter uses (lower is better) is
0\.056 per call if you say exactly that, 0\.057 if you say
90%, and 0\.058 if you say 99%. Saying 90 gives up almost nothing; saying 99 costs
more even when the situation really is that lopsided, and far more when it isn't, which is the usual human
error: in study after study, people's "90% sure" answers come true well under 90% of the
time.[^overconf] So 90 is a ceiling for beginners, not a law. When
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) shows that your 90% calls come true more than nine times in
ten, raise your ceiling to 95 for the empty-backfield and third-and-long snaps that earned it.

A small vocabulary helps you say the number fast:

| Say | Means | Typical use |
|:---------|:-----:|:----------------------------------|
| "Coin flip" | 50% | Nothing to go on: the formation was off screen, or the clues pull both ways |
| "Lean" | 55–60% | First-and-10 from a balanced look; one weak clue |
| "Probably" | 65–70% | The formation agrees with the situation |
| "Likely" | 75–80% | A strong formation clue and a situation that points the same way |
| "Near certain" | 85–90% | Third-and-long, an empty backfield, a two-minute drill when trailing |

### Layered predictions

Run or pass is the first layer, and after step 3 it's mostly decided. A good reader makes a second call on
the snaps where there's time, and states a confidence for it too:

- **On a likely pass:** the coverage family (man or zone; one-high or two-high after the snap), the rush
  (four, or five or more), or where the ball should go (the quick throw, the sticks, a shot).
- **On a likely run:** the direction (toward the strength, away from a shotgun back's offset, at the light
  side of the box) or the scheme family (gap, if a guard is cheating back to pull; zone is confirmed only at
  the snap, when the line steps together). The hash won't call the direction for you: runs from a hash went to
  the field and to the boundary about equally in 2025.

Second-layer calls are harder, and your confidence should show it. Their defaults come from base rates too.
In 2025 defenses sent five or more rushers on only 27% of dropbacks
(39% on third-and-7 to 10), so "four rush" is the default until a pressure tell moves
you off it. Zone was the coverage on about 69% of charted dropbacks, so "zone" is the
default, except near the goal line: man rose from 28% of dropbacks outside the red zone to
46% inside it, because a short field leaves zone defenders little deep space to sink into,
and tight coverage on every receiver is the natural answer to short throws. (FTN's man share jumps around
between seasons in a way that looks like charting rather than football, so treat these as rough.[^cov]) A
second-layer call at 60–70% is a good call; anyone who claims 90% on coverages before the snap is watching a
very predictable defense or not keeping score.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden you always know one of the two calls, your own. Watching a real game you know neither, and
neither does anyone on the field: the quarterback's pre-snap read *is* this checklist, and he gets it wrong
often enough that offenses build [hot routes](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) and post-snap reads
for the times he does. So a probability isn't a hedge. It is the most accurate description of what anyone,
including the players, knows before the snap.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"My 90% call missed, so I was wrong." Not necessarily: one in ten 90% calls *should* miss. You can't judge
a single probabilistic call by its outcome, only a pile of them. That's why the log matters, and why
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) scores a season of calls rather than a play. The mistakes to
look for are patterns: 90% calls that miss one time in three (overconfidence), or a log full of 55% calls
that come true 75% of the time (you know more than you're admitting).
:::

## Film room: one drive, nine snaps

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — the NFC Championship Game"}
**The game:** Rams at Seahawks, NFC Championship Game, January 25, 2026, at Lumen Field. Seattle, the NFC's
top seed (14–3), won 31–27 and two weeks later beat New England 29–13 in Super Bowl LX.[^nfc] In 2025 Seattle's
head coach was Mike Macdonald, its offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak (whose system comes from the Shanahan
family tree; see [Shanahan's Wide Zone Tree](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd)) and its
quarterback Sam Darnold.[^staff]

**The drive:** Seattle had gone up 24–13 early in the third quarter; the Rams answered with a touchdown to make
it 24–20 with 9:45 left in the quarter. After the touchback, Seattle drove 65 yards in nine snaps and scored on

**Why this drive:** it has a bit of everything the checklist is for: three different personnel groups, under
center and shotgun, an empty backfield, a screen against a blitz, play-action, a no-huddle snap, two third
downs and a red-zone touchdown, against a defense that played base, nickel and dime and three different
coverage labels.

**The sources:** every fact below comes from the public charting in nflverse;[^drive] the diagrams are
typical pictures of what was charted, not the film.

::: {#cell-fig-drive-trace .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.75))
n = len(DRV)
ys = np.arange(n)[::-1]
MARK = [dict(marker="o", s=36, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, label="situation only"),
        dict(marker="s", s=16, color=style.INK_2, label="+ personnel"),
        dict(marker="^", s=42, color=style.THIRD, label="+ formation"),
        dict(marker="D", s=16, color=style.INK_2, label="+ motion, tempo"),
        dict(marker="o", s=52, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="+ box: the final call")]
ax.axvline(0.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(0.5, n - 0.35, "coin flip", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
for y_, (i_, row) in zip(ys, DRV.iterrows()):
    pts = [row[f"p{k}"] for k in range(len(TRACE))]
    ax.plot(pts, [y_] * len(pts), color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    for k, (v, mk) in enumerate(zip(pts, MARK)):
        kw = {kk: vv for kk, vv in mk.items() if kk != "label"}
        ax.scatter([v], [y_], zorder=3 + k, **kw)
    ax.text(-0.02, y_, f"{i_ + 1}  {ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}, {row.yrdln}", ha="right", va="center",
            fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
    ok = row.hit
    ax.text(1.02, y_, ("✓ " if ok else "✗ ") + ("pass" if row.is_pass else "run") + f": {row.result}",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, color=style.THIRD if ok else style.DEFENSE_DARK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.1)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("chance of a pass, as the checklist goes on", fontsize=7.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
handles = []
for mk in MARK:
    face = mk.get("facecolor", mk.get("color"))
    edge = mk.get("edgecolor", mk.get("color"))
    handles.append(Line2D([], [], marker=mk["marker"], ls="", mfc=face, mec=edge, ms=np.sqrt(mk["s"]) * 0.95,
                          label=mk["label"]))
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.17), ncol=5, fontsize=6.4, frameon=False,
          handletextpad=0.3, columnspacing=1.0)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.24, right=0.72, bottom=0.2, top=0.95)
plt.show()
```

Now walk it the way you would live, step by step. The snap numbers match the log.

**Snap 1: first-and-10 at the Seattle 35, left hash.** 12 personnel (Kupp and Jake Bobo the receivers)
against base; under center, one back, motion: a run look, but only run\, 55%, because offenses
throw from it too. George Holani runs behind the right guard for three. ✓

**Snap 2: second-and-7.** Second-and-medium leans pass, but Seattle stays in 12 personnel with a second player
in the backfield, most likely a tight end lined up as an H-back (in the backfield, just off the tackle's hip).
Two backs under center swings the call back to run\, 60%. The Rams answer with a nickel, which
looks like the defense betting on a pass, until you notice *who* came on. On snap 1 the receivers were Kupp
and Bobo; now they are Kupp and Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the league's 2025 Offensive Player of the Year. On this drive
every snap with Smith-Njigba on the field drew a nickel or a dime, and every 12-personnel snap without him drew
base.[^jsn] The Rams were matching a player, not a digit: that's the "notice *which* receivers" of step 2. Kenneth
Walker loses two around the right end. The call was right; the run wasn't, and you're scoring your read, not
the offense.

**Snap 3: third-and-9 at the 36, right hash.** The run-or-pass question answers itself
(pass\, 90%), and everything after step 3 goes into the second layer. Seattle goes to 11 personnel
in the shotgun; the Rams go to dime (six defensive backs) with only five men in the box, a defense that wants to
keep everything in front of it and tackle short of the sticks. The base-rate calls say zone and a four-man rush,
and that's what came: four rushers, and a zone FTN labelled Cover 9, a number that means different things to
different staffs ([Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)); the figure draws
the Fangio meaning, a weak-rotation Cover 3 ([Fangio's Two-High Revolution](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)).
Darnold held the ball 2.8 seconds and found Kupp short to the left, toward the field, a throw FTN charted as a
checkdown: six yards in the air and six after the catch, a first down by three yards.

::: {#cell-fig-snap3 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def snap3():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dl = [("OLB1", "OLB", 1.0, -6.6), ("DT1", "DT", 1.0, -2.0), ("DE1", "DE", 1.0, 1.2), ("OLB2", "OLB", 1.0, 6.0)]
    dfn = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w, label="T" if pos == "DT" else "E") for k, pos, d, w in dl]
    dfn += [Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 5.5, 0.6),
            Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 7.5, -15.8, label="CB"), Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.5, 15.8, label="CB"),
            Player("ND", "DB", "def", 6.0, -9.6, label="$"), Player("DM", "DB", "def", 6.0, 9.6, label="D"),
            Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.0, -8.5), Player("SS", "SS", "def", 13.0, 8.5)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=46, to_go=9, ball_y="right")
    p.highlight("H")
    p.route("X", r.go(20)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12)); p.route("Y", r.dig(12, 8))
    p.route("H", r.path((5.0, 0.0), (5.6, 3.5), (6.0, 11.0)), speed=4.6)   # a short out, run flat to the sideline
    p.route("H", r.path((6.0, 0.6)), speed=6.5)                          # ...and up the field after the catch
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -0.4)])
    p.dropback(2.5)
    protect(p)
    engage(p, ("OLB1", "DT1", "DE1", "OLB2"))
    # Cover 9 drawn as a weak rotation: the left (weak) safety comes down, the right one runs to the middle
    p.drop("FS", (9.0, -5.0), speed=5.0)
    p.drop("SS", (17.0, 0.0), speed=6.0)
    p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 15.8), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 1.5)); p.drop("DM", (8.5, 11.5))
    p.drop("ND", (8.5, -12.5), speed=4.5)
    p.path("ND", [(9.0, -19.0)], speed=4.0, delay=2.8, absolute=True)   # drives on the throw
    p.read("Z")
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.8)
    return p


s3 = snap3()
```

Snap 3, third-and-9 from the right hash (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun, no motion; the Rams in dime with five in the box; four rushers; a zone labelled Cover 9; a checkdown thrown after 2.8 seconds to Cooper Kupp (H, ringed) on a short out to the left, toward the wide side of the field: six yards in the air and six after the catch for the first down. Illustrative: the alignments, the other routes, and the rotation, drawn as the weak-rotation Cover 3 meaning of 'Cover 9' (two-high before the snap, the safety away from the tight end coming down, three deep). Defensive letters: E, an end or edge rusher; T, a tackle; M, the one linebacker; $ and D, the nickel and dime backs; FS and SS, the safeties. What to notice: the quarterback's eyes (the green dashed line) start on the right, where Z's curl and Y's dig are covered by the underneath defenders sinking to the sticks, and only then does the ball go left; the conversion comes from the yards after the catch.
:::
:::


That's the usual shape of third-and-long: the run-or-pass call is free, the defense's plan is readable from
its personnel, and the play is decided by something you can't predict, a tackle made or missed. A second-layer
call of "zone, four rush, the ball goes short" was right, and that's as good as reading gets.

**Snap 4: first-and-10 at the 48, left hash.** Seattle goes heavy: 13 personnel (three tight ends, one
receiver), under center, two backs, motion. The Rams match with base and five linemen and edge rushers up front
(two of them listed on the roster as nose tackles), a seven-man box. The call is run\, 70%, as
confident as a first-down run call gets, and that leaves time for a second layer: *which way?* Under center
there's no shotgun offset to read, so the clues are the strength (the side with more tight ends, or the
H-back's side) and the light side of the box. The charting doesn't record which side those were, so this drive
can't score a direction call. Walker went behind the right guard for eleven. In your own log, write the
direction call anyway (`l2 right, 0.6`): your eyes record what the charting doesn't.

**Snap 5: first-and-10 at the Rams' 41.** The reverse picture: 11 personnel, shotgun, and **nobody in the
backfield**. An empty backfield is the strongest pass tell in the catalogue (95% of
2025 empty-backfield snaps were dropbacks), and the call is pass\, 85%. The second layer is the
interesting part. Empty leaves only five blockers, so a sixth rusher is unblockable and the quarterback has to
beat him with a quick throw; that's why empty is so often a quick-throw formation. The Rams rushed four and
played Cover 3, and Darnold checked the ball down to Holani, who had lined up outside the backfield as a
receiver, on a shallow cross for nine.

**Snap 6: second-and-1 at the 32, right hash.** The most interesting snap of the drive. Second-and-short is
the down where offenses take chances, because even a failed play leaves a manageable third down; from the
shotgun with 11 personnel it was a pass 57% of the time in 2025. The model
says run\, 55%. Why the disagreement? The model adds the down and the formation as separate
pushes and never learns that this particular pairing, the shotgun on second-and-short, throws more than the two
pushes suggest: at the formation step it says 44% where the raw rate is
57%. Narrow the raw rate to this exact look (one back, motion, six in the box)
and it falls to 49%, though on only 57 snaps. Either way it's close to
a coin flip, and there's a general lesson: when you know the base rate for the exact look, trust it over a sum of
clues. The second layer said zone (70%) and a four-man rush
(75%). The Rams played zone but sent five, and Darnold got the ball out in 0.7
seconds on a screen to Smith-Njigba, who caught it four yards *behind* the line, toward the field, and ran
sixteen yards after the catch. ✗ on run or pass, and a 55% call is allowed to miss: that is what 55% means.

``` {.python .cell-code}
def snap6():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = [Player("WDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, -5.8), Player("WDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -2.0),
           Player("SDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, 1.0), Player("SDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 5.8),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.5, 1.8), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 4.5, -2.2),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 5.0, -9.6), Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, -15.8, label="CB"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, 15.8, label="CB"), Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.5, 0.0),
           Player("SS", "SS", "def", 8.5, 9.6)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=78, to_go=1, ball_y="right")
    p.highlight("H")
    p.motion("Y", to=(-1.5, -5.6), speed=5.0)                # tight end across: three to the left
    p.motion("SS", to=(8.0, 2.0), speed=3.0)                 # the safety bumps over: a zone answer
    # defense: five rush, Cover 3 behind
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-3.5, 0.6), (-7.1, -2.8)], speed=5.0)  # at the line when the ball comes out, then wide
    p.drop("FS", (14.0, -2.0), speed=3.0)
    p.path("FS", [(15.0, -16.0)], speed=6.0, delay=0.5, absolute=True)
    p.path("LCB", [(3.6, -14.0)], speed=3.0, delay=0.3, absolute=True)   # comes up and meets X's block
    p.drop("RCB", (13.0, 15.0), speed=5.0)
    p.path("NB", [(1.5, -11.6)], speed=4.5, absolute=True)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 0.0))
    p.path("MIKE", [(10.6, -12.8)], speed=5.5, delay=0.6, absolute=True)   # the inside linebacker makes the tackle
    p.drop("SS", (8.5, -3.0), speed=4.0)
    # offense: the screen
    protect(p)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.5, 0.4)])
    p.route("H", r.path((-1.5, 1.6), (-2.5, 3.6)), speed=4.0)
    p.route("H", r.path((16.0, 2.4)), speed=7.0)
    p.block("X", pts=[(3.2, 0.9)], speed=3.0)
    p.block("Y", target="NB")
    p.route("Z", r.go(14))
    p.dropback(0.8)
    p.pass_to("H", t=0.7)
    return p


s6 = snap6()
```

Snap 6, second-and-1 from the right hash (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun with motion; the Rams in nickel with six in the box; five rushers (one of them a blitzer) and Cover 3 behind them; a screen to Jaxon Smith-Njigba (H, ringed) on the left, toward the field, thrown 0.7 seconds after the snap, caught four yards behind the line, sixteen yards after the catch, tackled by an inside linebacker. Illustrative: who motioned (here the tight end, Y, across to the left), which defender blitzed (here the Will linebacker, W), and the blocks. What to notice: the third panel, when the ball is already out and the blitzer has only reached the line; with him gone, the screen side has three Seattle players (X and Y blocking, H with the ball) against two Rams defenders, the corner and the nickel.
:::
:::


Why does a screen beat a blitz? Because every extra rusher is a defender who isn't covering anyone. This was a
perimeter screen, thrown at once: the blitzing Will was one fewer Ram on the outside, so the screen side had
three Seattle players against two defenders, and the ball was gone before the fifth rusher mattered. A pressure
call against a screen is the worst outcome for a defense, and it happens because the defense was guessing too:
second-and-1 from the shotgun is a coin flip for everyone. Could step 8 have warned you? The charting can't say
whether the Will showed his blitz before the snap, so the reconstruction doesn't draw a tell. If he did (a
linebacker creeping toward the line with one safety deep), your second-layer call should have moved from "four
rush" toward "five or more, ball out fast".

**Snap 7: first-and-10 at the Rams' 20.** Back to 12 personnel, under center, two backs, motion, against base
and a seven-man box. Every step says run: run\, 75%. It was play-action. Darnold faked the
handoff, left the pocket and, after 4.7 seconds, found the tight end AJ Barner short on the left for seven. ✗.
This is the miss you *should* have, the tendency-breaker built to beat the reader who believes the look: an
offense from the Shanahan tree lives on making its run and play-action looks identical
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). At
75% the call was honest. At 95% it would have been a misread. And the model
doesn't know it's Seattle; you would. From 12 personnel under center on first down, Seattle threw
42% of the time in 2025 (139 snaps), against
34% for the league, so a reader who copied the team's tendencies before kickoff
would have started this snap several points closer to pass.

**Snap 8: second-and-3 at the 13, no huddle.** Seattle hurried to the line in the same personnel, under center
with one back. The call is run\, 70%, and it missed again: a quick throw to Jake Bobo, out 0.6
seconds after the snap and aimed at a spot 1 yard behind the line, which FTN charts as a designed throw with no progression: a perimeter extension of the run game rather than a dropback. Incomplete. The second
layer split: in this spot (second-and-short in the red zone, four defensive backs) the 2025 base rates said man
(70%) and five or more rushers (80%). The Rams
did send five, but played Cover 3 behind them. Two run-call misses in a row, both passes from a run look, is not
bad reading; it's a play-caller deliberately working against his own tendency in the red zone. The
between-snaps habit (card line 13) is where you'd note it, and your next call from that look should drop
toward 55%.

**Snap 9: third-and-3 at the 13, left hash.** Shotgun, 11 personnel, motion: the model says
pass\, 75%. Third-and-short in the red zone is one of the few spots where man coverage is about as
common as zone (the 2025 base rate for this spot was man 55%), so the coverage
call was close to a coin flip. The Rams played zone, a Cover 6 (quarters to one side, Cover 2 to the other), set
the way Cover 6 usually is: quarters to the field, on the right, where Kupp was. They rushed four and got
interior pressure, but Darnold threw on time, 2.4 seconds after the snap, to a receiver in his progression
rather than a checkdown:[^read] Kupp on a short post, caught at the 6, six more yards after the catch,
touchdown. ✓

``` {.python .cell-code}
def snap9():
    off = offense("gun_2x2", strength="left")      # X wide right, H (Kupp) right slot, Y left slot, Z wide left
    dfn = [Player("WDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, -5.8), Player("WDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -2.0),
           Player("SDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, 1.0), Player("SDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 5.8),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.0, 1.5), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 4.0, -2.5),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 4.5, 7.4), Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 5.0, -15.8, label="CB"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 6.0, 15.8, label="CB"), Player("FS", "FS", "def", 10.0, -8.0),
           Player("SS", "SS", "def", 9.5, 7.0)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=97, to_go=3, ball_y="left")
    p.highlight("H")
    p.motion("Y", to=(-1.5, -5.4), speed=5.0)                 # short motion in to a wing
    p.motion("WILL", to=(4.0, -3.4), speed=1.5)               # a bump, not a chase: zone
    # offense
    p.route("H", r.path((4.0, 0.0)), speed=5.0)
    p.route("H", r.path((0.5, 1.2)), speed=5.0)               # a jab outside...
    p.route("H", r.path((4.0, -3.2)), speed=5.0)              # ...then the post, inside the nickel
    p.route("H", r.path((0.6, -1.2)), speed=1.0)              # finds the window in front of the safety
    p.route("H", r.path((6.5, -1.5)), speed=6.5)              # and runs it in
    p.route("X", r.fade(14)); p.route("Z", r.slant(2, 6)); p.route("Y", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -3.2)])                          # the back helps to the left
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    p.block("RG", pts=[(-1.4, 0.5), (-2.4, 0.4)], speed=1.5)  # beaten inside
    p.dropback(2.5)
    # defense: four rush; quarters to the right, Cover 2 to the left
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("SDT", pts=[(-2.0, 0.6), (-6.0, -0.2)], speed=2.6)  # through the B gap as the ball leaves
    p.drop("RCB", (12.0, 15.0), speed=4.5)
    p.drop("SS", (12.0, 12.0), speed=3.0)                      # #2 went inside: he helps on X's fade...
    p.path("SS", [(12.2, 9.4)], speed=4.5, delay=0.6, absolute=True)   # ...and comes back too late
    p.path("NB", [(4.6, 11.6)], speed=4.0, absolute=True)      # bites on the jab
    p.path("NB", [(9.5, 6.4)], speed=5.0, delay=0.9, absolute=True)
    p.drop("LCB", (3.0, -13.5), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -8.0), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -5.5)); p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 1.0))
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.4)
    return p


s9 = snap9()
```
